title: They mocked him before the battle even began.
paragraphs: They mocked him before the battle even began.

Not out loud—no, this wasn’t the kind of mockery you hear. This was quieter. Heavier. The kind that settles in the air when numbers don’t add up, when logic screams defeat, when everything visible says, “You don’t stand a chance.”
King Abijah stood facing an army twice his size.
Four hundred thousand against eight hundred thousand. Steel against overwhelming steel. Breathing men staring at death, knowing the odds had already chosen a winner.
But heaven hadn’t.
And that’s the part most people miss.
Because this wasn’t just a war between two kingdoms.
This was a collision between trust and pride… between covenant and rebellion… between God’s promise and human confidence.
And somewhere in the tension of that battlefield, a truth was about to be written so loud it would echo for generations.
A truth you might need right now more than you realize.
The Scriptures say in 2 Chronicles 13:3–5 that Abijah faced Jeroboam with half the army. Jeroboam, the king of Israel, had strength, numbers, strategy—and confidence rooted in what he could see.
But Abijah had something else.
He stood on Mount Zemaraim and cried out—not to his soldiers first, but to the truth.

“הֲלֹא לָכֶם לָדַעַת כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נָתַן מַמְלָכָה לְדָוִיד עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל לְעוֹלָם לּוֹ וּלְבָנָיו בְּרִית מֶלַח”
(Hălō lāḵem lāḏa‘aṯ kî YHWH ’ĕlōhê Yiśrā’ēl nāṯan mamlāḵāh ləḏāwîḏ ‘al-Yiśrā’ēl lə‘ōlām lō ûləḇānāw bə·rîṯ melaḥ)
“Do you not know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt?”
A covenant of salt.
Not temporary. Not fragile. Not negotiable.
Salt in ancient times symbolized permanence—preservation that could not be undone.
Abijah wasn’t trusting his army.
He was standing on a promise.
And that’s where everything shifts.
Because Jeroboam had numbers, but he had abandoned the altar.
He had replaced priests. Created false worship. Built a system that looked religious but was disconnected from God’s presence.
And this is where the danger still lives today.
You can look strong… and still be spiritually empty.
You can build something impressive… and still be standing outside the will of God.
You can win in the eyes of people… and still be losing where it actually matters.
Jeroboam set an ambush behind Abijah. Strategically brilliant. Completely devastating.

From the front, an army.
From the back, a trap.
It was over.
At least, that’s what logic would say.
But Scripture says something different happened next.

“וַיִּצְעֲקוּ אֶל־יְהוָה”
(Vayyits‘ăqū ’el-YHWH)
“They cried out to the LORD.” — 2 Chronicles 13:14
Not strategized.
Not negotiated.
Not panicked.
They cried out.
Because when you run out of options, you finally discover where your strength was supposed to come from all along.
And God answered.
The text says God struck Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah.
Not Abijah’s skill.
Not Abijah’s numbers.
God.
That’s the part that humbles every prideful heart.
Because victory didn’t come from superiority.
It came from surrender.
And maybe that’s the part of your story you’ve been resisting.

You’ve been trying to outwork what only God can overcome.
Trying to fix what only grace can heal.
Trying to win battles God never asked you to fight alone.
But here’s what Abijah understood…
God doesn’t need favorable odds.
He needs faithful hearts.
The Greek word often used in the New Testament for victory—“νίκη” (níkē)—doesn’t just mean winning. It carries the idea of overcoming, prevailing despite resistance.
And that kind of victory never starts in your hands.
It starts in your surrender.
Because Jesus Himself became the ultimate picture of this.
He didn’t conquer Rome with armies.
He walked into death.

Publicly shamed.
Beaten.
Mocked.
A scandal.
The Greek word “σκάνδαλον” (skándalon) means a stumbling block… something offensive… something that doesn’t make sense.
That’s what the cross looked like.
And yet, that scandal became salvation.
That defeat became redemption.
That ending became everything.
From scandal… to grace.
Just like Abijah’s battlefield.
Just like your story.
You might feel surrounded right now.

By mistakes.
By fear.
By consequences.
By voices telling you it’s already over.
But the same God who answered a cry on a battlefield is still listening.
And He hasn’t forgotten His covenant.
He hasn’t changed His nature.
He hasn’t lost His power.
The question is not whether God can win your battle.
The question is whether you’ll finally stop fighting it your way.
Be honest…
How many times have you tried to handle things on your own first… and only cried out when everything collapsed?
How many hidden battles are you still pretending you can manage?
How many wounds are you covering instead of surrendering?
Because healing begins where honesty starts.
And someone else reading your comment might realize they’re not alone.
And if you’re serious about growing deeper in your walk with Christ… if you’re tired of surface-level faith and ready for real transformation…
Stay close to truth.
Because discipleship isn’t built in moments—it’s built in daily surrender.
And for those who want to go deeper…
There’s something waiting for you.
If this message moved you… if it stirred something deeper… don’t ignore that.
Step into it.
Because supporting what spreads the Gospel isn’t just generosity…
It’s obedience.
And it helps more souls encounter the same truth that just reached you.
Because one day, you’ll realize…
The battle that looked impossible was actually the place God was waiting for your surrender.
